question: What is the leading chronic health condition that results in lower limb amputation?
explanation: Diabetes damages blood vessels and nerves over time, making wounds hard to heal and often leading to tissue death. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h1)

question: Why does severe peripheral vascular disease often lead to an amputation?

options.A: Blocked arteries prevent oxygen and nutrients from reaching tissues, causing cell death.
options.B: High blood pressure forces the limb to swell until the skin splits open.
options.C: Excess fluid builds up in the muscles and causes the bone to snap.
options.D: Weakened veins allow blood to pool and turn into dangerous blood clots.

explanation: Think of it like a plant without water—when blood flow is cut off, the tissue lacks oxygen and dies, which can create gangrene that requires surgery. Great job learning the basics! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h1)

question: What is a transtibial amputation commonly known as?
explanation: The tibia is the shin bone, so a transtibial procedure removes the limb below the knee joint. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h2)

question: Why would a surgeon leave an amputation wound open instead of stitching the skin right away?

options.A: To allow drainage and prevent trapping severe infection inside the wound
options.B: To stretch the skin flaps so they cover a larger area of bone
options.C: To give the patient time to practice moving the joint before closure
options.D: To make it easier to fit a temporary plastic cast on the bone

explanation: If there's an infection present, closing the skin immediately would trap bacteria inside and cause abscesses. Leaving it open temporarily keeps things safe! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h2)

question: What emergency item must always be kept right at the bedside after an amputation surgery?
explanation: A tourniquet is kept at the bedside just in case there is sudden, heavy bleeding from the surgical site that needs immediate stopping. Safety first! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h3)

question: On day one after a below-knee amputation, what should the nurse do to help prevent joint stiffness (contractures)?

options.A: Encourage the patient to cross their legs while sitting up.
options.B: Limit the time the residual limb rests elevated on pillows.
options.C: Apply a heavy sandbag directly over the end of the stump.
options.D: Keep the residual limb propped up on pillows for the entire day.

explanation: Keeping the stump propped up for too long causes the muscles to tighten in a bent position. We want to keep those joints flexible! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h3)

question: When wrapping a residual limb with an elastic bandage, where should the pressure be tightest?

options.A: At the bottom end of the stump
options.B: Equally tight all the way up
options.C: Near the top of the joint

explanation: Wrapping tighter at the bottom (distal end) pushes fluid upward and helps shape the limb into a neat cone, which makes fitting a prosthesis much easier later. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h4)

question: Why should a patient avoid putting lotion on their residual limb before wearing a shrinker sock?

options.A: Oily substances make the prosthesis slide off during walking exercises.
options.B: Lotion dissolves the elastic fibers inside the special compression bandage.
options.C: Trapped moisture creates a breeding ground for bacteria and skin breakdown.
options.D: Moisturizers stop the surgical incision from closing completely.

explanation: Lotion plus a tight wrap equals a warm, wet space where bacteria and fungi love to grow. Keeping the skin clean and dry prevents rashes and breakdown! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h4)

question: What is the main difference between phantom limb sensation and phantom limb pain?

options.A: Pain only happens during the day, while sensation occurs exclusively while sleeping.
options.B: Sensation means the limb is still there, while pain means the nerve has died completely.
options.C: Pain is purely psychological, while sensation is caused by poor blood flow.
options.D: Sensation involves normal feelings like tingling, while pain involves burning or shooting hurt.

explanation: Phantom sensation is just a harmless awareness that the limb is missing (like feeling an itchy toe), whereas phantom pain is actual uncomfortable, shooting distress. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h5)

question: A patient complains of a burning pain in a leg that was surgically removed last week. How should you, as the nurse, respond?

options.A: Acknowledge the pain as real neuropathic discomfort and report it for treatment.
options.B: Tell the patient this feeling is temporary and will vanish within a few hours.
options.C: Suggest that the patient is imagining things because of anxiety over surgery.
options.D: Gently remind the patient that the leg is gone so the pain cannot actually exist.

explanation: Phantom pain is very real! It comes from the cut nerve endings trying to heal, so always validate your patient and get them the relief they need. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h5)

question: Which muscle groups need the most strengthening when a patient is learning to use crutches after an amputation?
explanation: Using crutches without a lower limb means the arms, shoulders, and chest have to do all the heavy lifting. Time for some push-ups! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h6)

question: Why is early physical therapy encouraged soon after amputation surgery?

options.A: To stretch the skin until it breaks open for drainage
options.B: To force the brain to stop feeling the missing limb
options.C: To prevent joint stiffness and maintain muscle strength
options.D: To prevent the patient from ever needing a wheelchair

explanation: Getting moving early keeps the joints flexible and stops the muscles from getting weak before it's time for a prosthesis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h6)

question: What emotional reaction do patients very commonly experience right after losing a limb?

options.B: Grief and a sense of loss

explanation: Losing a body part is a huge life change. Patients go through a normal grieving process, and it's our job to support them with empathy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h7)

question: Why is it so helpful for a recovering patient to talk to another person who has also gone through an amputation?

options.A: It stops the patient from ever experiencing phantom limb pain again.
options.B: It gives practical proof that a fulfilling life and independence are possible.
options.C: Friends who share the same diagnosis speed up physical wound healing.
options.D: Peer visitors are trained medical professionals who can change dressings.

explanation: Seeing someone else thrive after the same experience gives wonderful hope and makes the patient feel much less alone. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h7)

question: What is the most important home safety change to make in the bathroom after an amputation?

options.A: Replacing all porcelain fixtures with plastic ones
options.B: Removing the bathroom door to improve airflow
options.C: Installing grab bars near the toilet and shower
options.D: Painting the bathroom walls a bright, cheerful color

explanation: Wet bathroom floors plus new mobility challenges spell danger. Grab bars and shower seats keep baths safe and independent! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h8)

question: Why should loose throw rugs be removed from a patient's home after surgery?

options.A: They easily slide underfoot and cause dangerous falls.
options.B: They prevent the wheelchair wheels from rolling smoothly.
options.C: They trap moisture and cause the home humidity to rise.
options.D: They block the medical equipment from plugging into the wall.

explanation: Unsecured rugs love to slip on smooth floors, making them a major tripping hazard for anyone learning to get around with new supports. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h8)
